endorsements.title: Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use
endorsements.quote: Physicians, staff, and patients must all be aware of the risks of mis- and disinformation when engaging with generative and other forms of AI.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Determine whether the use of the solution is consistent with the implementing organization’s risk tolerance and whether the solution offers an appropriate way to achieve stated goals in light of identified risks.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Use organizational risk tolerance to evaluate acceptable risks and performance metrics and decommission or retrain pre-trained models that perform outside of defined limits.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Requiring AI vendors to provide a model card or equivalent documentation as a condition of contract execution for any AI solution.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether defining an organizational AI risk tolerance, and declining or deferring AI that exceeds it, reduces the deployment of AI with unacceptable residual risk. The recommendation rests on two framework statements from CHAI and NIST that address risk tolerance directly, plus two related endorsements that do not.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. Two of the four endorsements address risk tolerance directly. The other two concern awareness of misinformation and vendor model cards, which are adjacent practices rather than the threshold-setting practice itself.

The NIST Generative AI Profile tells organizations to use risk tolerance to judge acceptable performance and to decommission or retrain models outside defined limits. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks whether a solution fits the organization's risk tolerance. Both are voluntary frameworks written as should statements, and neither carries regulatory force on its own.

commentary.research_gap: No study has examined whether health systems with a written AI risk tolerance decline, defer, or decommission tools at different rates than systems without one. No study has examined whether such thresholds are associated with fewer patient harms. A useful first study would compare governance decisions and post-deployment incidents across organizations with and without defined thresholds. It would also record how thresholds are set and who sets them.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether organizational risk thresholds account for risks that fall more heavily on these groups, or whether safety-net systems have the capacity to set and apply such thresholds.
